original_question: Suppose ℵ1 < κ < λ = c and the positive relation \( inom{\kappa}{\omega} 	o  inom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2\) holds. After forcing with the Lévy collapse P = Levy(κ, λ), is it possible that in the extension the full positive relation for κ and ω fails?
target_in_paper: Problem 2.19 in Section 2 ("Countable problems"): if \aleph_1 < \kappa < \lambda = \mathfrak{c} and \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \to \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2, does forcing with \mathbb{P}=\mathrm{Levy}(\kappa,\lambda) make \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 in V^{\mathbb{P}}?
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s exact formulation. It correctly has the hypotheses \aleph_1 < \kappa < \lambda = \mathfrak{c}, assumes the strong polarized relation \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \to \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2, uses the Lévy collapse \mathrm{Levy}(\kappa,\lambda), and asks whether in the forcing extension the full strong relation for the pair (\kappa,\omega) can fail. That is exactly the content of Problem 2.19 rather than the weaker follow-up Problem 2.20.
missing_details: State explicitly that \mathfrak{c} means the ground-model continuum 2^{\aleph_0}.
Name the relation as the strong polarized relation, matching Definition 0.1.

Define the notation \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \to \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2: for every coloring c: \kappa \times \omega \to 2 there are A \subseteq \kappa and B \subseteq \omega with |A|=\kappa and |B|=\omega such that c\!\upharpoonright(A\times B) is constant.
State the failure in the extension in the exact symbolic form \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 in V^{\mathbb{P}}.
Indicate that \mathbb{P}=\mathrm{Levy}(\kappa,\lambda) is the Lévy collapse used in the paper’s formulation.

If you want the paper-faithful scope, mention that this problem appears as a generalization motivated by the sentence immediately before it: treating the case \mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{s}<\mathfrak{c} by collapsing \mathfrak{c} via Lévy collapse after Problem 2.18.
refined_question: Assume \aleph_1 < \kappa < \lambda = \mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0} in the ground model, and assume the strong polarized relation \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \to \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 holds; that is, every coloring c: \kappa \times \omega \to 2 admits sets A \subseteq \kappa and B \subseteq \omega with |A|=\kappa and |B|=\omega such that c\!\upharpoonright(A\times B) is constant. Let \mathbb{P}=\mathrm{Levy}(\kappa,\lambda) be the Lévy collapse. Is it possible that in the forcing extension V^{\mathbb{P}} the strong polarized relation fails, i.e. \binom{\kappa}{\omega} \nrightarrow \binom{\kappa}{\omega}^{1,1}_2?
justification: The draft matches Problem 2.19 essentially verbatim. The paper first defines the strong polarized relation in Definition 0.1, then in Section 1 records background results for the countable case, including Theorem 1.2 and the splitting-number criterion Theorem 1.6. Immediately before Problem 2.19, the authors ask in Problem 2.18 whether \binom{\mathfrak p}{\omega} \to \binom{\mathfrak p}{\omega}^{1,1}_2 holds exactly when \mathfrak p<\mathfrak s, and then say that one may try to treat the case \mathfrak p=\mathfrak s<\mathfrak c by collapsing \mathfrak c with Lévy collapse; this leads directly to Problem 2.19. Your wording targets the full relation’s failure after the collapse, so it is Problem 2.19, not the weaker mixed-target Problem 2.20. Theorem 1.3 is only broader background about the uncountable/supercompact analogue and is not the direct source of your question.
